processing: Best known pan-fired as kamairicha rather than steamed; heating in a pan stops oxidation and gives the toasty aroma this cultivar handles well.
harvest_season: Spring, about a day after Yabukita; first flush is usual for single-cultivar lots.
appearance_dry: As is usual for kamairicha, curled and twisted olive-green leaf rather than needles.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale gold, typical of pan-fired Japanese green tea.
appearance_wet: Olive-green opened leaves, as with other kamairicha.
taste_profile: Smooth and vegetal with sweet, nutty notes and a mellow umami, plus the distinctive pan-fired fragrance.

brewing.notes: Kamairicha takes hotter water than sencha, and it pours clean because the leaf stays whole. Do not steep it as hard as a black tea or the toasted note turns harsh.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, as is usual for Japanese green tea, ideally drunk within a year. It is mostly seen as single-cultivar kamairicha from Miyazaki, such as organic lots from Gokase.
description:
Minekaori is a cultivar for pan-fired green tea, grown in Miyazaki, Kumamoto and Oita. Most Japanese cultivars are judged as sencha, so one that shines as kamairicha is a bit of a specialist.

The leaf goes through a hot pan instead of a steamer. As sencha it has not impressed, because its aroma shifts considerably when steamed, while as kamairicha it keeps a fragrance of its own.

Expect a smooth cup with nuttiness, sweetness and a soft umami. Use water around 80°C, hotter than you would for most sencha, and do not worry about the leaf being intact in the pot: that is how kamairicha should look.

Buy it from Kyushu mountain growers who name the cultivar. Try it beside an Okuyutaka kamairicha, since the two have been compared directly in Kumamoto.
history: Minekaori came from a Yabukita × Unkai cross at the Miyazaki prefectural agricultural research station and was registered in May 1988 as Japanese tea cultivar number 38. A Kumamoto trial reported in 1996 found that, in highland gardens, its pan-fired tea had a strong and good kamairicha character and that mature fields yielded well. It is also credited with good cold tolerance and about 30% more yield than Yabukita.
